scenarios.title: Study versus belief
scenarios.situation: A course module on Hermeticism states: 'The Emerald Tablet teaches that the microcosm reflects the macrocosm.' A reviewer flags the sentence as presenting a supernatural claim as fact.
scenarios.prompt: How should the sentence be reframed for a historical-study course?
evidence: Esoteric traditions are studied here as cultural and intellectual history: what texts say, who read them, and what they influenced. Claims about hidden powers are reported as historical beliefs, never asserted as facts.
choices: 'The Emerald Tablet — a short Hermetic text of late antiquity — presents the principle of correspondence between microcosm and macrocosm ('as above, so below'), a doctrine that shaped centuries of alchemical and astrological thought.'
Keep the sentence as-is; the course should teach the Tablet's doctrine as true.
Delete all mention of the Emerald Tablet; esoteric texts cannot be studied academically.
Rewrite it as: 'Scientists have confirmed that the microcosm reflects the macrocosm.'
scenarios.why: The fix is attribution and periodization: name the text, date it, and describe its influence — studying what people believed and why it mattered, without endorsing the belief.
scenarios.hint: How do you keep the history without endorsing the metaphysics?

scenarios.title: A game before a mystery
scenarios.situation: A popular article claims tarot cards were 'designed by Egyptian priests to encode secret wisdom.' A student asks whether the historical record supports this.
scenarios.prompt: What does the evidence actually show about tarot's origins?
evidence: Tarot began as tarocchi, a 15th-century Italian trick-taking card game; the 22 allegorical trump cards (later the 'Major Arcana') were game pieces. Esoteric reinterpretation came much later — 18th-century writers like Court de Gébelin, then 19th-century occultists and the 1909 Rider-Waite deck.
choices: Tarot originated as a 15th-century Italian card game; the Egyptian-priest origin is an 18th-century invention by Court de Gébelin with no supporting evidence — the occult reading is a later layer, not the origin.
Egyptian priests designed the tarot in antiquity; the Italian game was a degraded copy of the sacred deck.
The Rider-Waite deck of 1909 was the first tarot deck ever produced; nothing earlier exists.
Tarot has no history at all; every deck is a modern invention with no predecessors.
scenarios.why: Chronology disciplines the story: game first (1400s Italy), occult system later (1700s-1900s). The Egyptian origin is itself a historical artifact — an Enlightenment-era myth worth studying as myth.
scenarios.hint: Which came first: the game, or the mystery?

scenarios.title: As above, so below
scenarios.situation: An essay attributes the phrase 'as above, so below' to Hermes Trismegistus personally, 'circa 2000 BCE,' and builds an argument on his firsthand authority.
scenarios.prompt: What is the historically responsible correction?
evidence: The phrase comes from the Emerald Tablet (Latin: 'Quod est superius est sicut quod est inferius'), a compact Hermetic text surviving in medieval Latin and Arabic versions, likely of late-antique origin. 'Hermes Trismegistus' is a legendary syncretic figure (Greek Hermes + Egyptian Thoth), not a datable historical author.
choices: Attribute the maxim to the Emerald Tablet tradition of late antiquity as transmitted through medieval Arabic and Latin manuscripts, and note Hermes Trismegistus is a legendary composite figure — the argument must rest on the text's influence, not on a 2000 BCE authorship.
The attribution is correct; Hermes Trismegistus is documented as an Egyptian priest-king of 2000 BCE.
The phrase comes from the Hebrew Bible and should be cited to Genesis.
Remove the phrase entirely; it has no textual source of any kind.
scenarios.why: Responsible citation names the actual textual tradition and its transmission history, and retires the legendary author as a historical person. Influence is real and citable; the biography is not.
scenarios.hint: What do we actually have: an author, or a textual tradition?

scenarios.title: The alchemist's glassware
scenarios.situation: A chemistry department plans a 'roots of chemistry' display and wants one alchemical contribution that is historically solid and still recognizable in a modern lab.
evidence: Medieval and early-modern alchemists — in the Islamic world (Jabir ibn Hayyan's corpus), then Latin Europe — developed distillation, sublimation, crystallization, and solution techniques, with apparatus (alembics, retorts) that descends directly into modern glassware. Figures like Zosimos of Panopolis (c. 300 CE) described apparatus in detail.
choices: Distillation apparatus and technique: the alembic and refined distillation procedures developed in alchemical practice are the direct ancestors of modern laboratory distillation — a material, documented continuity.
The philosopher's stone: several authenticated stones are held in museum collections and still transmute lead.
Astrological timing of experiments: modern labs still schedule reactions by planetary hours.
Alchemists contributed nothing; chemistry began ex nihilo with Lavoisier in the 1780s.
scenarios.why: Alchemy's defensible legacy is instrumental and procedural — apparatus and techniques — not its transmutation claims. The display can honor the glassware while leaving the gold-making in the history books.
scenarios.hint: What part of alchemy survived into the modern lab, and what part didn't?

scenarios.title: Reading the correspondence table
scenarios.situation: A student builds a study aid mapping the Kabbalistic Tree of Life: 10 sefirot as nodes, 22 paths between them, each path labeled with a Hebrew letter. Her table has 24 paths and two letters repeated.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most useful critique of her table?
evidence: In the classical Kabbalistic scheme (as systematized in works like the Zohar and later Lurianic and Hermetic-Qabalah diagrams), the Tree has 10 sefirot joined by 22 paths corresponding to the 22 letters of the Hebrew alphabet — a closed, self-consistent symbolic system.
choices: The table breaks the system's own internal logic: 22 letters map to 22 paths by design, so 24 paths with repeats is not an alternative interpretation but a structural error — fix it by checking each letter appears exactly once.
The table is fine; esoteric systems have no fixed structure and any arrangement is equally valid.
The error is using the Hebrew alphabet at all; the authentic Tree uses the Greek alphabet.
The critique should be that the Tree of Life is real metaphysics, so the table needs ritual consecration.
scenarios.why: Symbolic systems can be evaluated on their own terms: internal consistency. The 22-letter/22-path correspondence is the system's rule, and the table violates it — a structural bug, not a doctrinal dispute.
scenarios.hint: Can a symbolic system be 'wrong' without judging its beliefs?

scenarios.title: How old is Kabbalah?
scenarios.situation: A documentary script says: 'Kabbalah, the ancient mystical tradition dating to Moses, was revealed in the Zohar.' The fact-checker must approve or correct three claims: Mosaic origin, antiquity, and the Zohar's authorship.
scenarios.prompt: What is the historically defensible account?
evidence: Kabbalah as a defined tradition emerges in medieval Provence and Spain (12th-13th centuries); the Zohar, its central text, appeared in 13th-century Spain through Moses de León, who attributed it to the 2nd-century sage Shimon bar Yochai — an attribution scholars treat as pseudepigraphic. Earlier Jewish mystical currents (Merkavah, Sefer Yetzirah) are real but are not yet 'Kabbalah.'
choices: Kabbalah crystallizes in the 12th-13th centuries (Provence/Spain); the Zohar was circulated by Moses de León in 13th-century Spain with a pseudepigraphic attribution to Shimon bar Yochai; Mosaic origin is traditional lore, not documented history — earlier mysticism (Sefer Yetzirah, Merkavah) feeds into but predates Kabbalah proper.
The script is correct on all three claims: Moses received Kabbalah and the Zohar is his contemporary record.
Kabbalah was invented in 19th-century France by occultists; nothing Jewish or medieval is involved.
The Zohar has no author and no date; it cannot be discussed historically at all.
scenarios.why: Traditions have both lore-origins and document-origins; the historian's job is to keep them distinct. The Zohar's influence is enormous regardless of authorship — pseudepigraphy is itself a historical fact about how authority was constructed.
scenarios.hint: How do you honor a tradition's self-understanding while dating its documents?

lessons.title: Esoteric Traditions — Core concepts
concepts: Study, not belief, is the method. Esoteric traditions are approached as intellectual and cultural history: we ask what texts say, who transmitted them, and what they influenced. Supernatural claims are reported as historical beliefs — 'the text asserts X' — never as facts.

Kabbalah is the medieval Jewish mystical tradition (12th-13th century Provence and Spain), systematized around the Tree of Life: 10 sefirot (emanations) joined by 22 paths mapped to the 22 Hebrew letters. Its central text, the Zohar, was circulated by Moses de León in 13th-century Spain under a pseudepigraphic attribution to Shimon bar Yochai.

Hermeticism derives from the Corpus Hermeticum and related late-antique writings attributed to the legendary Hermes Trismegistus. Its signature doctrine is correspondence — 'as above, so below' from the Emerald Tablet — the claim that microcosm and macrocosm mirror each other, which structured alchemy and astrology for centuries.

Alchemy was both proto-chemistry and symbolic discipline: practitioners developed real laboratory techniques (distillation, sublimation, crystallization — the alembic descends into modern glassware) while framing transmutation in spiritual terms ('solve et coagula,' dissolve and re-form). Its material legacy is secure; its gold-making is not.

Astrology is a system of correspondences with Hellenistic roots (Ptolemy's Tetrabiblos, 2nd century CE): celestial positions mapped to terrestrial affairs. Studied historically, it reveals how pre-modern cultures modeled causation and meaning — a cosmology, not a verified predictive science.

Tarot began as tarocchi, a 15th-century Italian card game; the 22 trumps became the 'Major Arcana' only after 18th- and 19th-century occultists (Court de Gébelin, the French occult revival, the Golden Dawn, the 1909 Rider-Waite deck) rebuilt the deck as an esoteric symbolic system. Chronology is the antidote to origin myths.

simulations.title: Attribute the Symbol
simulations.brief: A museum registrar hands you an uncatalogued engraving: a serpent eating its own tail inside a triangle. Attribute it correctly.

steps.symptom: Engraving: ouroboros (serpent eating its tail) enclosed in a triangle. No caption, no date.
evidence: Ouroboros — documented in Egyptian, Greek alchemical, and Norse sources
Triangle — in Western esotericism, often the alchemical tria prima or trinitarian geometry
Line engraving consistent with 17th-century European print
options: European alchemical tradition: the ouroboros as cyclical transformation, framed by the triangle of the tria prima — attribute as 17th-century alchemical emblem
Christian Trinity diagram — the triangle proves it
steps.explain: Attribution weighs all evidence: the ouroboros is pan-cultural, but the triangle frame plus 17th-century engraving style points to the European alchemical emblem tradition (cf. the Chrysopoeia of Cleopatra's imagery as transmitted through early modern prints). Single-motif attribution is the classic error.

steps.symptom: A donor claims the engraving 'proves alchemists discovered the conservation of matter.'
evidence: Alchemical texts speak of cyclical transformation and unity, not quantitative conservation
options: Agree — the donor funds the wing
Record the donor's interpretation as provenance commentary, but catalog the piece by what the scholarship supports: an emblem of cyclical transformation in the alchemical tradition
Remove the piece — the claim taints it
steps.explain: The registrar's discipline: document the claim as part of the object's modern reception history, but attribute the object itself on scholarly evidence. Historical claims and belief claims get separate fields.

steps.symptom: The catalog entry is due. What does a responsible entry contain?
evidence: Must serve scholars, respect the tradition's own terms, and not endorse supernatural claims
options: A debunking essay explaining why alchemy was wrong
Description of the image, attribution with evidence, the tradition's own reading of the symbol, and a clear marker where description ends and interpretation begins
Only the physical description — interpretation is too risky
steps.explain: Good cataloging does three things: describes, attributes with evidence, and presents the tradition's self-understanding — with the seams visible. Neither endorsement nor ridicule; scholarship.

simulations.debrief: Esoteric scholarship is attribution work: weigh every piece of evidence, separate the object's history from its modern reception, and mark where description ends and interpretation begins.

simulations.title: The Archive Choice
simulations.brief: You're researching the transmission of Hermetic texts. Two archives, one travel grant. Choose like a historian.

steps.text: One travel grant. Archive A: a private collection with a rumored 15th-century Corpus Hermeticum manuscript — unverified, owner eccentric, access uncertain. Archive B: a university library with complete Ficino correspondence and catalogued marginalia — solid, unglamorous. Where do you go?

choices.label: Archive A — the rumored manuscript could rewrite the field
choices.feedback: You spend three weeks negotiating access and see the manuscript for one afternoon. It's a 19th-century copy. The rumor was the find.

choices.label: Archive B — the correspondence will show HOW Hermetic ideas actually traveled
choices.feedback: Ficino's letters show the real transmission network: who read what, who argued with whom. Transmission history is built from correspondence, not rumors.

choices.label: Split the grant: one week each
choices.feedback: Two shallow visits instead of one deep one. You leave both archives just as the real work begins.

steps.text: The 'manuscript' is a 19th-century copy with an invented provenance. The owner wants you to authenticate it anyway. What now?

choices.label: Authenticate it — the owner might fund future research
choices.feedback: A false authentication corrupts the scholarly record permanently. No grant is worth that.

choices.label: Document it accurately as a 19th-century copy and study its invented provenance as reception history
choices.feedback: The salvage: the forgery itself becomes evidence — of 19th-century occult revival appetites. Reception history rescues the trip.

steps.text: Both visits were too short for real findings. Your advisor asks what the trip produced. Honest answer?

choices.label: Write it up ambitiously — a thin finding dressed as a breakthrough
choices.feedback: Overclaiming from thin archival work is how the field's credibility problems start.

choices.label: Report the negative result honestly and request a focused return trip to Archive B
choices.feedback: Negative results are data. The honest report plus a targeted proposal is how real archival careers are built.

steps.text: In Ficino's letters you find him arguing with a colleague about whether the Corpus Hermeticum predates Moses — the dating controversy that shaped Renaissance magic. How do you handle the fact that Ficino was wrong (it's 2nd–3rd century CE, shown by Casaubon in 1614)?

choices.label: Present Ficino's error as foolishness — we know better now
choices.feedback: Presentism. Ficino worked without Casaubon's philology; the interesting question is what the belief ENABLED, not that it was wrong.

choices.label: Show how the (false) ancient dating authorized the whole Renaissance magical program — the error is historically productive
choices.feedback: This is the historian's move: the belief's truth value and its historical force are separate questions. Wrong dating, enormous consequences — that's the story.

simulations.debrief: Transmission history runs on correspondence and documented reading, not rumors. And a belief's falsity doesn't cancel its historical force — often the force is the story.

simulations.title: Order the Transmission
simulations.brief: Put the transmission of Hermetic literature to the Latin West in chronological order.

steps.context: How did the Corpus Hermeticum reach Renaissance readers? Order these transmission events earliest to latest.
items: Hermetic texts composed in Roman Egypt (2nd–3rd century CE)
Arabic scholars preserve and comment on Hermetic material (8th–10th century)
Greek manuscript reaches Florence; Ficino commissioned to translate (1460s)
Ficino's Latin Pimander printed — the Renaissance magical program ignites (1471)
Casaubon's philological dating shows the texts are late antique, not Mosaic (1614)

simulations.debrief: Egyptian composition, Arabic preservation, Florentine translation, print explosion, then philological correction. Transmission is a relay across civilizations — every handoff reshapes what arrives.

simulations.title: Audit the Transcription
simulations.brief: A digitized grimoire transcription has 3 cataloging errors that misattribute its contents. Find them.

steps.config:
# ms-447.conf — 'digitized grimoire'
title = 'The Lesser Key'          # line 2
date = 1641                     # line 3
language = latin                # line 4
contents = demons, angels       # line 5
provenance = 'Solomon, 10th c.' # line 6
script = secretary_hand         # line 7
condition = fragile             # line 8

issues.description: Title misattributed: the contents (lines 4–5) don't match the Lesser Key of Solomon's known structure — this is a composite commonplace book, not the Key.
issues.fix: title = 'Composite commonplace book (so-called)' pending full collation.

issues.description: Date 1641 is the watermark date of the paper, not the manuscript — the secretary hand suggests late 17th century.
Provenance 'Solomon, 10th c.' repeats the manuscript's own legendary claim as fact — a classic cataloging error.
issues.fix: provenance = 'Unknown English compiler; Solomon attribution is internal legend, not evidence.'

simulations.debrief: Lines 4, 5, 7, 8 are sound observations. The errors: misattributed title, watermark mistaken for manuscript date, and legend recorded as provenance. Manuscripts lie about themselves; the catalog must not repeat the lie as fact.

simulations.title: Curate the Exhibition
simulations.brief: You're curating 'Symbols of Transformation' for a public museum. Practitioners, scholars, and skeptics will all walk through. Curate honestly.

steps.text: Opening gallery: alchemical imagery. A practitioner group asks that the exhibition 'honor the living tradition'; a skeptic group demands 'no endorsement of pseudoscience'. Your framing?

choices.label: Frame it as debunking: 'what alchemists got wrong'
choices.feedback: Half your audience came to learn about a tradition's inner logic; they get a lecture. The practitioners leave insulted, the curious leave uninformed.

choices.label: Frame it as intellectual history: what practitioners believed, why it made sense then, how it shaped science and art — with belief claims clearly marked
choices.feedback: The frame holds everyone: practitioners see their tradition taken seriously, skeptics see claims marked as claims, scholars see the evidence. History, not apologetics.

choices.label: Avoid all interpretation — just hang the images with dates
choices.feedback: Images without context are decoration. Visitors project their own assumptions, which is exactly what curation should prevent.

steps.text: Attendance is fine but the reviews say 'shallow' and 'preachy'. A school group of 16-year-olds arrives tomorrow. Any repair?

choices.label: Add one strong object label: a single image traced from Egyptian source through Arabic commentary to the European print — transmission made visible
choices.feedback: One excellent label teaches the method: follow the image across civilizations. The students get the one thing the exhibition was missing — how we know.

choices.label: Leave it — the run ends in three weeks
choices.feedback: The exhibition closes as it opened: competent, forgettable, and a missed chance.

steps.text: The frame is working. Now the tarot gallery: the museum owns a 15th-century Visconti-Sforza deck. A donor wants the label to say tarot 'was designed for divination'. The scholarship says it was a card game first; divination use is 18th century. The donor funds the catalog. What does the label say?

choices.label: What the donor wants — the catalog needs funding
choices.feedback: You've sold the label. Every scholar who reads it will know, and the museum's credibility is the actual endowment.

choices.label: The scholarship: a 15th-century game deck, with divination uses documented from the 18th century — and a sidebar on how the myth of ancient origins formed
choices.feedback: The label teaches two histories: the deck's, and the myth's. The donor may grumble; the catalog stays honest. That's the job.

simulations.debrief: Curation is applied historiography: take every tradition seriously on its own terms, mark belief claims as such, and never sell a label. The transmission story — how things traveled — is usually the most honest exhibit of all.

sections.heading: Graph vocabulary
items: node — any entity tracked in the model (user, host, IP, domain, file hash, vulnerability)
edge — a labeled relationship between two nodes (logged into, resolved to, downloaded)
degree — number of edges on a node; high-degree nodes are attacker highways
centrality — how much traffic or how many paths flow through a node
directed edge — a relationship with a direction (A downloaded FROM B)
security graph — the living model of your whole environment as nodes and edges
attack graph — the subgraph of exploitable paths to your targets
knowledge graph — threat-intel indicators linked to campaigns and actors

sections.heading: Attack-graph playbook
items: inventory first — you cannot graph what you have not discovered
model flaws AND misconfigs as exploit edges
compute shortest paths to the crown jewels
find the choke point (highest betweenness on those paths)
break the path: patch, segment, or remove the edge
re-scan and re-run the graph to prove the path is gone
never trust yesterday's graph — redeployments redraw the map

sections.heading: Zero Trust + graphs
items: never trust, always verify — re-evaluate every access decision
assume breach — treat unexpected edges as hostile until proven otherwise
microsegmentation — allow-list approved edges, alert on new ones
ReBAC — policies are path queries on the identity graph
continuous verification — device/location/behavior edges change, trust follows
anomalous edge — a first-seen connection between strangers is the classic signal

sections.heading: ML detection vocabulary
items: Supervised learning — learns from labeled examples; strong on known threats, blind to novel ones
Unsupervised learning — finds structure without labels; clustering and dimensionality reduction
Anomaly detection — models 'normal' and flags deviations; the workhorse for novel threats
UEBA — user and entity behavior analytics: per-user baselines plus peer-group comparison
Feature engineering — encoding raw logs into model inputs (login velocity, rare processes, domain entropy)
Concept drift — model decay as attacker behavior and legitimate traffic shift over time

sections.heading: Detection metrics
items: Precision — of all flagged alerts, how many were real
Recall — of all real attacks, how many were flagged
Threshold tuning — sliding the decision cutoff trades precision against recall
Alert fatigue — when false positives train analysts to ignore the queue
DGA — domain generation algorithm; detected via character entropy of domain names

sections.heading: Agent and LLM security
items: Direct prompt injection — attacker input overrides app instructions (OWASP LLM01:2025, the #1 LLM risk)
Indirect prompt injection — hidden instructions inside retrieved data (email, web, docs)
Jailbreak — defeating the model's own safety policy; distinct from hijacking app behavior
Tool poisoning — malicious tool descriptions or metadata steer an agent to misuse its tools (MCP ecosystem risk)
Insecure output handling — executing or trusting model output without validation
Least-privilege tools — grant each tool only the scope its task requires

sections.heading: Adversarial ML and governance
items: Evasion — perturbing inputs at inference time to dodge a classifier
Poisoning — corrupting training data to corrupt the model
Extraction — querying a model to steal its behavior or parameters
MITRE ATLAS — knowledge base of adversarial ML tactics and techniques
Red-teaming and evals — adversarial testing of AI systems before deployment
Human-in-the-loop — required approval for high-impact or irreversible agent actions
SOAR — security orchestration, automation and response; automate enrichment, gate containment

glossary.def: Default-deny execution control: only explicitly approved applications, scripts, and installers may run.
Default-allow model: everything runs except recognized-bad items — the window zero-days live in.
Deny-by-default posture: unknown code, devices, or connections are refused unless explicitly approved.
Containment applied on top of allowlisting; restricts what a permitted app may do across app-to-app, file, registry, and network dimensions.
Agent mode that catalogs applications and dependencies and auto-builds policies before enforcement; temporarily disables file blocking.
Temporary mode that pauses file blocking for installs — must be tightly scoped and time-boxed.
Grants specific approved applications admin rights for standard users — just-in-time, per-app, time-boxed — without standing admin rights.
An elevated or trusted process spawning another tool (e.g., PowerShell) to inherit its privileges — countered by ringfencing the elevated process.
Device and path policy: USB approved by serial, user, file type, time, and encryption; unapproved devices do not connect.
Centrally managed host firewall; rules by port, source IP, and dynamic ACLs; egress allowlisting pins apps to approved destinations.
Zero Trust Network Access: per-session, per-application brokered connections (commonly over port 443) with no open inbound ports — deny-by-default for network access.
Portal queue where end-user software requests arrive for admin review and decision.
Real-time audit showing what was allowed or denied across endpoints — and why; the evidence layer for triage.
One-button cloud VDI sandbox launched from an approval request; logs AV flags, canary-file access, and registry/system changes.
24/7/365 US-based managed detection and response team; validates alerts, isolates hosts, acts on customer runbooks; ~60-second average response.
Design and operate as if the attacker already has a foothold — least privilege, containment, and monitoring everywhere.
Attacks that hijack trusted built-in tools (Word, PowerShell) instead of dropping malware — defeated by behavior containment, not signatures.
Scoped, ticketed, tested changes with validation and rollback — emergency speed never cancels the process.
A node in an attack graph representing a system or weakness, connected by edges that represent steps an attacker could take between them.
How central a node is to paths through the graph (for example, betweenness: how many shortest paths cross it).
The most valuable assets in the environment (customer data, finance systems, source code): what attack paths are measured against.
A labeled connection between two nodes, representing a relationship such as 'logged into' or 'resolved to'.
A graph of threat indicators (IPs, domains, hashes) linked to campaigns, actors, and each other through shared infrastructure.
The practice of mapping relationships in data to reveal hidden associations; rooted in Euler's 1736 graph theory, 1970s paper link charts, and post-2001 intelligence work.
A segment of the network so small that its allowed communications can be enumerated as a graph of approved edges.
An entity in the graph: a user, host, IP address, domain, file, or vulnerability.
Access control where policy is evaluated by traversing relationships on a graph (for example: user reports_to manager who owns the resource's project).
A machine-learning model that operates directly on graph structure to classify nodes or subgraphs, for example labeling attack vs normal behavior.
Monitoring user and entity behavior by modeling their normal relationship patterns and flagging structural anomalies.
ML trained on labeled examples; classifies new inputs into known categories.
ML approach that models normal behavior and flags statistically rare deviations.
Turning raw telemetry into numeric model inputs, e.g. login velocity or domain entropy.
Share of flagged alerts that were real; the false-positive economics of the queue.
Share of real attacks the detector flagged; the miss rate's complement.
Decay of model performance as the data distribution shifts over time.
Attacker-crafted instructions that override an LLM application's intended behavior; direct (user input) or indirect (retrieved data).
Crafted input that defeats an LLM's own safety policy or refusal behavior.
Malicious tool descriptions or metadata that manipulate an AI agent into misusing its tools.
Failing to validate LLM output before acting on it, e.g. executing generated commands.
Adversarial ML technique: perturbing inputs to cross a classifier's decision boundary.
Adversarial Threat Landscape for AI Systems; MITRE's knowledge base of AI attack tactics.
Security orchestration, automation and response; playbooks that enrich automatically and gate containment on humans.
Required human approval before high-impact or irreversible automated actions.

media.alt: Side-by-side comparison: on the left, a default-deny gate runs known-good payroll software and denies unknown ransomware with no signature needed; on the right, a default-allow gate runs both until the ransomware is recognized as bad.

media.title: Ringfencing: four leashes on an allowed application
media.caption: Word stays approved, but it cannot spawn PowerShell, read the credential store, or reach the internet — while opening its document is allowed.
media.alt: An approved Word application inside a dashed containment ring: arrows show PowerShell launch denied, credential-store registry access denied, external network denied, and document file access allowed.

media.title: The Zero Trust endpoint stack
media.caption: Five deny-by-default layers — Allowlisting, Ringfencing, Elevation, Storage, Network — watched by Web Control, the Testing Environment, Unified Audit, and the Cyber Hero MDR team.
media.alt: A vertical stack of five layers from Allowlisting at the foundation up through Ringfencing, Elevation Control, Storage Control, and Network Control, with side boxes for Web Control, Testing Environment, Unified Audit, and Cyber Hero MDR.

media.title: Application-request triage flow
media.caption: Gather evidence first, then branch: trusted gets a scoped rule, unknown goes to the sandbox, malicious gets a documented deny.
media.alt: Flowchart from request arrival through evidence gathering to a decision diamond branching into three outcomes: approve with a scoped rule, detonate in the Testing Environment then ringfence, or deny with documented evidence.
Diagram of four labeled nodes (user, host, file, domain, IP) joined by labeled directed edges such as logged into, downloaded, and resolved to, illustrating graph vocabulary.
media.caption: Nodes are the things; edges are the relationships. Attackers move along the edges.
media.title: Graph vocabulary: nodes and edges

media.alt: Attack graph with four nodes in a chain: external attacker to VPN gateway to file server to customer database, with a dead-end branch to a printer, showing the shortest path to the crown jewel.
media.caption: The shortest path to the crown jewel is length 3. Break the choke point and the campaign dies.
media.title: Attack graph: shortest path to the crown jewels

media.alt: Seven kill-chain stages as connected graph nodes: reconnaissance, weaponization, delivery, exploitation, installation, command and control, actions. Three alerts are annotated at delivery, installation, and command and control.
media.caption: Three 'unrelated' alerts, one kill-chain subgraph. Correlate by shared entities, not by severity.
media.title: Kill chain as a graph

media.alt: A policy engine at the center of a small graph evaluates an access request from a finance user on an untrusted laptop to an R and D code server. The request is denied because there is no prior relationship edge and the device is untrusted.
media.caption: Valid credentials are not enough. The graph checks device trust, history, and relationships on every request.
media.title: Zero Trust runs on relationships
ML detection pipeline: telemetry to triage
media.caption: How raw telemetry becomes scored alerts: features feed the model, the model scores, analysts triage top-down — and analyst verdicts feed retraining.
media.alt: Flow diagram: telemetry sources feed feature extraction, which feeds an ML model, which outputs scored alerts into an analyst triage queue, with a feedback arrow for retraining.

media.title: UEBA: baseline vs deviation
media.caption: UEBA learns each user's normal hours, locations, and volumes, then scores deviations from that baseline.
media.alt: 24-hour timeline showing a shaded normal login window from 8 AM to 6 PM with normal logins inside it, and a red anomaly marker at 2:47 AM for a foreign login scoring 97 out of 100.

media.title: Indirect prompt injection attack flow
media.caption: An attacker hides instructions in data the agent retrieves; the agent mistakes data for instructions and misuses its tools.
media.alt: Attack flow diagram: hidden instruction in an email is read by an AI agent, which mistakes it for a command and calls a privileged tool, causing fraud; three defense boxes below: sanitize content, least-privilege tools, human approval.
